title: Live trading: My AI agent vs Claude vs GPT vs copying the top 10 traders on Binance, OKX and Hyperliquid.
author: Mr_Hodlerr
selftext:
Bitcoin gave every strategy a real test this week. On Nov 4 it dipped to $75,601, then closed at $80,428 (+4.0%). On Nov 5 it gave it all back and closed at $75,969 (-5.5%). It's the second time in three weeks a breakout reversed the very next day: Oct 21 was the highest close of the month, and Oct 22 fell 3.2%.

Chop like this is where trading strategies get tested: you buy the breakout and get stopped out at the low. So here's how my AI agent did against Claude, GPT and copy trading the top human traders, all live.

**The setup**

\- Three live battles, $50,000 each, standings after every daily close.

\- The AIs trade bitcoin and ether only, spot, no leverage, one decision per daily close, same fees and same data.

\- Trading battle- Claude since Oct 9. GPT since Nov 3. Copy trading since Nov 2. ($5,000 copying each of the top 10 traders by 30 day return on Binance, OKX and Hyperliquid.)  


**Standings**

Vs Claude, since Oct 9:

\- Botsfolio AI $48,427 (-3.15%), worst drop 3.7%

\- Claude Opus 5.5 $46,226 (-7.55%), worst drop 8.6%

\- Claude Fable 5.1 $46,209 (-7.58%), worst drop 8.6%

\- Holding BTC + ETH $45,319 (-9.36%), worst drop 10.8%



Vs GPT, since Nov 3:

\- Botsfolio AI $49,718 (-0.56%), worst drop 1.0%

\- Holding $49,011 (-1.98%), worst drop 6.9%

\- GPT-6 Astra $48,272 (-3.46%), worst drop 3.5%

\- GPT-6 Sol $48,021 (-3.96%), worst drop 4.0%



Vs copy trading, since Nov 2:

\- Copying OKX's top 10 $52,444 (+4.89%), worst drop 6.3%

\- Botsfolio AI on altcoins $50,308 (+0.62%), worst drop 0.7%

\- Copying Hyperliquid's top 10 $49,852 (-0.30%), worst drop 3.9%

\- Botsfolio AI on bitcoin and ether $49,750 (-0.50%), worst drop 1.0%

\- Holding $49,552 (-0.90%), worst drop 6.7%

\- Copying Binance's top 10 $38,820 (-22.36%), worst drop 27.7%

OKX's copiers lead that one so far. 



Every trade and every model's note is on the live trading pages:

comments.author: Dependent-Ocelot908
comments.body: It says AI has no leverage and trades spot. I assume copy traders are taking big leverage and are doing both long/short trades too while AI is long only. So is it fair?

replies.author: Mr_Hodlerr
replies.body: Yes. The point of this trading battle is to see what works and how the journey is. Taking leverage and not taking leverage is also a part of a trading strategy.

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
Fun experiment, but one month on a falling market mostly measures one thing: how much crypto each player held. Everything that sat more in cash looks better, and the ranking would likely flip in a rising month.

A fairer scorecard would be:  
\- Return vs a benchmark with the same average exposure. If Botsfolio averaged 30% in BTC/ETH, compare it to 30% hold, 70% cash, not to 100% hold.  
\- Number of decisions. Around 20 to 28 daily decisions per player is far too few to separate skill from luck. Rough rule: you'd need a few hundred independent decisions before differences of a few percent mean anything.  
\- For copy trading: picking the top 10 by 30-day return is selecting on last month's luck. The Binance group at -22% is a great illustration of that, honestly the most useful result in the post.

Would be genuinely interested in the exposure-matched numbers if you post a follow-up.

replies.author: Mr_Hodlerr
replies.body:
Thanks. I see your point, especially about exposure and the fact that one month of data is too short to draw any real conclusions.

The way I see the benchmark is that it's also a test of different strategies. For example, holding cash and deploying less when confidence is low is itself a strategy, compared to simply buying and holding regardless of market conditions.

My bigger question is: as a retail trader, what should I actually do? Should I just buy and hold, use AI, copy trade, or follow some other strategy? Which approach actually works? The idea is to test different options and see what happens if I follow one approach versus another.

I also agree that the live trading data needs time to build. I wanted to make everything public from day one, including the trackers, so that 6–12 months from now we'll have a real track record to look at and can start seeing what works and what doesn't.

For context, in the backtests, the median yearly gain was higher than buy and hold across 94 different starting points. But backtests are one thing; I want to establish a genuine live trading record and see how the strategies perform over time.

And on your point about copy trading, that's exactly the kind of thing I want to test. If there's another strategy that most retail traders can realistically access and follow, I'm happy to add it to the trading battle. Let me know what you'd suggest.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Fair framing, and making it public from day one is the right call.

On "what should retail actually do": in my experience the honest answer is boring. Most retail traders would do better with a simple rule they actually stick to than with anything clever. So I'd add a few cheap, followable baselines to the battle, because those are what any strategy really has to beat:

1. Fixed mix with rebalancing: e.g. 50% BTC/ETH, 50% cash, rebalanced monthly. If an AI's "deploy less when confidence is low" can't beat a constant 50/50, the confidence isn't adding anything.  
2. DCA: same amount bought every week, no selling. What most people realistically do.  
3. A simple trend rule: hold when price is above its 200-day average, cash when below. One line, decades of history, a classic for a reason.

Those three answer your exposure question too, since they let you see whether a strategy beats a dumb version of the same average exposure.

One caution on the backtest: 94 starting points sounds like a lot, but if they're rolling windows over the same history, they overlap heavily and share the same few big bull and bear runs. Effectively that's a handful of independent periods, not 94. Median-beats-hold across overlapping windows can come almost entirely from sitting out one or two crashes.

replies.author: Mr_Hodlerr
replies.body: I will make these 3 rules and open a live trading battle, thanks. Will see if the AI can beat the dumb version or not.

replies.body: Write me DM with your results

comments.author: spoidercide
comments.body:
If you're comparing technical trading strategies, the real measure is in the entries and exits, not just the final dollar return. Every trade should be evaluated in terms of risk-to-reward (R), win rate, expectancy, and drawdown. Making $1,000 while risking $5,000 is completely different from making $1,000 while risking $200.

Without normalizing for risk, you're just comparing account balances and potentially making bad strategies look good. It's not about the price or the money made. It's about the underlying factors driving those returns and whether the decisions demonstrate a repeatable statistical edge.

replies.author: Mr_Hodlerr
replies.body: Its more of what would actually make more money than buy and hold with less pain whether its technical, fundamental, copying etc. In the end I am trying to find what makes money with least pain and headache.
